title: Japan Unveils World's First Hydrogen Engine for Large Commercial Vessels | Sada Elbalad
description:
Japan has unveiled what its developers describe as the world’s first hydrogen-fueled engine designed for large commercial vessels, marking a significant step toward reducing greenhouse-gas emissions from maritime transport.
Japan Engine has completed production of the 6UEC35LSGH, the first large marine commercial engine developed to operate on hydrogen.
The engine was unveiled to project stakeholders at Japan Engine’s main plant earlier this month.
The technology is being developed as part of Japan’s broader effort to introduce lower-emission propulsion systems for commercial shipping while advancing the use of hydrogen as a marine fuel.
The next phase of the project will see the hydrogen engine installed aboard a 17,500-deadweight-ton multi-purpose vessel being built by Onomichi Dockyard Co., Ltd.
text:
Japan has unveiled what its developers describe as the world’s first hydrogen-fueled engine designed for large commercial vessels, marking a significant step toward reducing greenhouse-gas emissions from maritime transport.

The engine, developed through a collaboration between Japan Engine Corporation, Kawasaki Heavy Industries, Ltd., and Yanmar Power Solutions Co., Ltd., is part of a project to develop marine hydrogen engines and marine hydrogen fuel supply systems under Japan’s Green Innovation Fund Next-Generation Vessel Development Project, led by the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO).

Japan Engine has completed production of the 6UEC35LSGH, the first large marine commercial engine developed to operate on hydrogen. The engine was unveiled to project stakeholders at Japan Engine’s main plant earlier this month.

Factory testing showed that the engine achieved a hydrogen co-firing rate of at least 95%, resulting in a reduction of greenhouse-gas emissions of more than 95% compared with conventional heavy fuel oil-powered engines, according to the project developers.

The technology is being developed as part of Japan’s broader effort to introduce lower-emission propulsion systems for commercial shipping while advancing the use of hydrogen as a marine fuel.

The next phase of the project will see the hydrogen engine installed aboard a 17,500-deadweight-ton multi-purpose vessel being built by Onomichi Dockyard Co., Ltd.

The vessel is being constructed for Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Ltd. (MOL) and MOL Drybulk Ltd. under the Blue Harmony project.

Operational testing of the hydrogen-powered engine aboard the vessel is scheduled to begin in April 2028, providing an opportunity to assess the technology under actual maritime operating conditions.

Japan’s classification society ClassNK will conduct safety assessments throughout the engine’s development, as well as during the vessel’s design, construction and operational stages.

MoU signed for wind-assisted LNG carrier project

Korean Register (KR) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HD HHI), UK-based wind propulsion technology company BAR Technologies, and the Liberian International Ship & Corporate Registry (LISCR) to jointly develop a 174K LNG carrier equipped with the WindWings wind-assisted propulsion system.

The agreement was signed on 15 September at Gastech 2026 in Bangkok and aims to assess the technical feasibility and safety of applying wind-assisted propulsion technology to LNG carriers as the global shipping industry accelerates its transition toward decarbonisation.

The project will focus on a 174K LNG carrier developed by HD HHI featuring a forward accommodation arrangement. By positioning the crew accommodation block toward the bow, the design provides additional space on the upper deck, creating an opportunity to integrate BAR Technologies’ WindWings system.

WindWings uses large, rigid wing sails installed on a vessel to harness wind as supplementary propulsion. By reducing reliance on the vessel’s main propulsion system, the technology can lower fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions while improving overall energy efficiency.

Under the collaboration, HD HHI will lead the vessel’s basic design and design review, while BAR Technologies will provide technical data covering the arrangement and specifications of WindWings, structural strength, operational concepts and expected fuel savings.

KR, together with LISCR, will assess the safety and technical suitability of the design against applicable rules and international requirements. Based on the outcome of the assessment, KR will also consider granting Approval in Principle (AIP), supporting the application and future commercialization of wind-assisted propulsion technology on LNG carriers.

Hongryeul Ryu, chief technology officer of HD HHI, said: “We have continued to develop innovative hull forms and arrangement concepts for LNG carriers to advance environmentally friendly ship technologies. Through this project, we aim to integrate wind-assisted propulsion technology into our forward accommodation LNG carrier design, further enhancing the competitiveness of next-generation, low-emission LNG carriers.”

John Cooper, CEO of BAR Technologies, said: “We already have WindWings deployed across 10 bulkers and tankers, with 23 WindWings collectively saving approximately 100 tonnes of CO2 per day. We look forward to extending the application of WindWings to next-generation gas carriers, establishing a robust foundation for safe commercialisation, and providing shipowners with a genuinely attractive environmental solution.”

Kyujin Yeon, executive vice president of KR, said: “Through this joint development project, KR will assess the safety and technical suitability of applying wind-assisted propulsion to this LNG carrier design against applicable rules and international requirements, with a view to granting AIP. By working closely with the shipyard, technology provider and flag administration, KR will continue to support the safe and reliable adoption of innovative technologies that contribute to the maritime industry’s decarbonisation.”

Alfonso Castillero, CEO of the Liberian International Ship & Corporate Registry, added: “This JDP reflects the Liberian Registry’s proactive approach to supporting the safe and responsible advancement of innovative maritime solutions. By assessing wind-assisted propulsion for LNG carriers from an early design stage, the partners can help translate the decarbonisation challenge into practical opportunities for improved efficiency, future-ready ship designs and competitive advantage, without compromising safety or quality.”

text:
K Shipbuilding and Lloyd's Register have signed a memorandum of understanding to design a 50,000 deadweight ton ethanol fueled medium range tanker, the companies said in a joint press release. K Shipbuilding will lead vessel design, while Lloyd's Register will evaluate the ship's arrangement, stability, structural requirements and fuel tank integration. The goal is to secure Approval in Principle and produce a design competitive in the global product tanker market.

Approval in Principle would confirm the concept's preliminary compatibility with applicable maritime rules. It would not represent a vessel order, a completed engineering package or a commitment from a shipowner. No owner, engine supplier, construction timeline or fuel provider has been named yet.

Ethanol's Lower Energy Density Could Shrink Tanker Cargo Space

Medium range tankers already move ethanol and other liquid fuels between regional markets, giving the segment a production and transport network that some newer marine fuels still lack. Burning that cargo as propulsion fuel is a separate commercial question. It would require agreements covering ownership, fuel quality, customs treatment and charter party terms, plus separate storage and delivery systems to keep fuel from contaminating cargo.

Ethanol also carries less energy per unit of volume than conventional marine fuel. A ship running on it may need larger tanks or more frequent refueling, and space set aside for propulsion fuel typically reduces the cargo capacity that generates revenue on a product tanker. How K Shipbuilding handles that tradeoff will help determine whether the design holds up on longer routes.

Shared Chemistry With Methanol Could Speed Ethanol Adoption

Ethanol shares chemical properties with methanol, and some methanol capable engines may be able to burn it with limited retrofitting. Maersk has already completed trial voyages running a methanol capable vessel entirely on ethanol, and Vale is among the companies now evaluating ethanol fueled ships of its own. Owners already weighing the cost and supply constraints tied to methanol bunkering may see ethanol as a cheaper option built on similar equipment.

Ethanol holds roughly 35% more energy by volume than methanol and can cost less than green methanol supplies. A dual fuel or alcohol flexible tanker could appeal to owners more than an ethanol only vessel, since it would limit exposure to a single fuel market. Lloyd's Register and K Shipbuilding have not disclosed a proposed engine configuration.

Carbon intensity will also shape how owners buy ethanol. Emissions vary by feedstock, farming practice and refinery energy use, so verified low carbon supply is likely to command a premium over chemically identical but higher carbon fuel. That could put shipping in competition with road fuel and aviation fuel buyers for the same low carbon ethanol, and it could concentrate early bunkering around established production centers in Brazil and the U.S. Gulf Coast.

In August, the U.S. Grains & BioProducts Council hosted a high-level delegation of senior Panamanian governmental and maritime sector leaders to examine how U.S. bioethanol can serve as a feedstock for sustainable marine fuel (SMF), while also informing Panama’s efforts on maritime decarbonization and supporting its broader national energy transition objectives.

USGBC Latin America (LTA) Regional Ethanol Strategy Lead Federico Salcedo, USGBC LTA Regional Ethanol Consultant Marcelo Velazquez and USGBC Manager of Global Ethanol Programs Emma Freebairn escorted the team during its visits to Illinois and Texas.

“Panama holds a strategic role in global shipping as steward of the Panama Canal and as a host of one of the world’s largest ship registries. As the maritime sector advances toward its decarbonization goals under the International Maritime Organization’s greenhouse gas strategy, Panama is well positioned to evaluate technically and commercially viable low-carbon marine fuel options,” Salcedo said.

“This program consolidated technical knowledge, strengthened institutional relationships and provided Panamanian officials with firsthand evidence and contacts to support maritime decarbonization while building confidence in ethanol as a viable low-carbon marine fuel.”

After arriving in Chicago, the group visited the University of Illinois-Chicago’s Energy Resources Center, where they met with Dr. Steffen Mueller and representatives from Growth Energy, a USGBC member, to discuss the U.S. ethanol industry, market developments and the role of ethanol in emerging low-carbon fuel pathways and agricultural sustainability. Later, Argonne National Laboratory welcomed the team for an overview of the latest research being conducted in the biofuels sector, including the GREET model.

Marquis Energy, a USGBC member, offered a tour of its ethanol plant in Hennepin the next day for a closer look at the ethanol production process, carbon capture techniques and the ethanol export value chain. Finally, USGBC Past Chairman Mark Wilson met the group at his farm in Toulon to observe his corn crop and learn about the climate-smart agricultural practices used by U.S. farmers.

In Houston, the team visited Advario and Eco-Energy, a USGBC member, for a tour of its liquid bulk storage facilities and export terminal to better understand the export logistics of U.S. biofuels. Next, Everllence showcased its line of engines and how they are ready for large-scale SMF adoption.

title: The Week in Alt Fuels: From promises to timelines - engine.online
description:
More concrete timelines are making ammonia bunkering look less like a pipe dream.
The Shenghang Yongle, described as the world's first operational ammonia bunker vessel, has put the fuel back in the spotlight.
Rotterdam, which completed a pilot transfer last year, expects its first ammonia bunker deliveries in 2026-2027.
So while questions around safety, fuel availability and real-world operating experience remain, more concrete timelines are bringing ammonia bunkering much closer to reality.
In other alt fuels news this week, class society American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) has approved the concept design of a 22,000-cbm LNG bunker vessel developed by Hanwha Power.
text:
More concrete timelines are making ammonia bunkering look less like a pipe dream. But recent leaks underscore the safety concerns as plans move closer to reality.

IMAGE: Aerial view of the Port of Hamburg in Germany. Getty Images

Chinese shipping firm Shenghang Shipping's converted ammonia carrier has achieved operational readiness as a bunker vessel after receiving certification for ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering from China Classification Society.

The 5,500-cbm vessel, Shenghang Yongle, was originally built as a liquefied gas carrier and has been converted to deliver liquid ammonia to other vessels through ship-to-ship bunkering. The companies have not disclosed where the vessel will be deployed or which port will host its first commercial ammonia bunker operation.

The Shenghang Yongle, described as the world's first operational ammonia bunker vessel, has put the fuel back in the spotlight. But the bigger picture is taking shape across several regions, with ports setting dates for bunker pilots, suppliers lining up fuel, and infrastructure being developed.

Asia is furthest along, with ammonia already delivered to vessels at two ports.

Lotte Fine Chemical has bunkered ammonia to vessels in South Korea's Port of Ulsan, and signed an agreement with Amogy in September to explore further ammonia bunkering there. A port tugboat was also bunkered with green ammonia at COSCO's Dalian terminal last year.

Pilbara Ports plans to carry out an ammonia bunker pilot this year. Rotterdam, which completed a pilot transfer last year, expects its first ammonia bunker deliveries in 2026-2027.

In Singapore, Itochu plans live bunker demonstrations in the fourth quarter of 2027, using a vessel due for delivery that September. Yara and Golden Island are expected to supply the fuel.

Terminal operator Azane Fuel and bunker supplier Equinor plan to start truck-to-ship ammonia deliveries in Norway in the second half of this year.

Azane Fuel and producer Yara Clean Ammonia are developing their first ammonia bunker facility at Fjord Base in Florø, Norway. The terminal will include one of Azane's floating bunker barges, capable of carrying 650 mt of ammonia. It has received a permit for up to 416 bunker transfers/year.

The Florø facility will be followed by bunker infrastructure in Risavika and Mongstad by 2029.

MB Energy has a permit to build a large-scale ammonia import terminal at the Port of Hamburg, with commercial operations planned for 2029. The project will include a new tank for temporary ammonia storage and upgraded vessel and barge berths that could eventually support ammonia bunkering. Planned throughput is around 600,000 mt/year.

Fertiglobe will look at supplying ammonia through the terminal, and may take a stake in it. Hamburg Port Authority has meanwhile introduced safety and operational guidelines for ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering and is considering adding an ammonia bunker barge.

Trafigura, CF Industries and TFG Marine are targeting ammonia bunkering in the US Gulf Coast and Northwest Europe. Elsewhere, India's VO Chidambaranar Port and Oman's Sohar are also gearing up for ammonia bunker operations later this decade.

Belgian shipping firm CMB.Tech is also developing ammonia storage and bunker infrastructure at Walvis Bay in Namibia.

The company has not disclosed when the terminal is expected to become operational, but said it will support its planned fleet of more than 40 ammonia-capable vessels. “The facility will provide critical infrastructure for green ammonia producers, off-takers, and traders, lowering barriers to entry and supporting the development of a robust green ammonia value chain in Southern Africa,” it said.

But despite the more concrete timelines and growing confidence around ammonia bunkering, some hurdles still stand between these early pilots and a mature bunker market.

Ammonia has been loaded and unloaded as cargo for decades, giving the shipping industry experience it can draw on.

But bunkering could involve more frequent transfers in a wider range of locations and operating conditions than conventional cargo handling. Its toxicity therefore means bunker operations will require careful handling, crew training and robust safety and emergency procedures.

Recent industrial accidents have offered stark reminders of those risks.

An ammonia leak at a seafood processing facility in Tamil Nadu in June killed 18 of the 83 workers affected. A more recent leak in Jordan's Aqaba industrial area injured 11 people and prompted a precautionary evacuation at the industrial complex.

On 13 September, an ammonia leak at a fertiliser plant in Basra's Khor Al-Zubair industrial area in Iraq killed two and injured 114 people, including workers and nearby residents.

Another hurdle is fuel supply.

Bunker buyers will need access to sufficient supplies of low- and zero-emission ammonia for the fuel to deliver meaningful emissions reductions. Whether enough green ammonia will be available by 2030 to meet demand from the future fleet remains an open question.

So while questions around safety, fuel availability and real-world operating experience remain, more concrete timelines are bringing ammonia bunkering much closer to reality.

In other alt fuels news this week, class society American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) has approved the concept design of a 22,000-cbm LNG bunker vessel developed by Hanwha Power. It will be able to carry both LNG and ammonia.

US-based startup Demeter Energy plans to build a 100,000 mt/year bio-methanol production plant at the Port of Manatee in Florida. The fuel is expected to be produced from woody biomass and other organic waste and go to bunkering and other sectors.

Class society Lloyd's Register (LR) has partnered with South Korea's K Shipbuilding to develop a 50,000 dwt ethanol-capable tanker.

By Konica Bhatt

text:
Europe’s largest green hydrogen project is being built in southwest Spain – Moeve

The first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley will include 300 MW of electrolysis and require investment of over €1 billion. Moeve expects to create more than 8,000 jobs during its development.

Moeve has begun construction in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva, on the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, a project the company presents as the largest of its kind in Europe and which aims to place Spain in a central position in the development of this new energy industry.

The first phase, called ‘Onuba’, will initially have 300 MW of electrolysis capacity, with the option of adding a further 105 MW, and will involve a total investment of more than €1 billion, including the associated infrastructure and a photovoltaic plant for self-consumption.

During the development, construction and commissioning phases, Moeve estimates that the project will create more than 8,000 direct jobs, as well as indirect and induced employment along the entire value chain, and will support activity at more than 400 small and medium-sized enterprises and local self-employed workers.

Moeve’s chief executive, Maarten Wetselaar, quoted in a statement, said:

Once again, we are turning ambition into a tangible reality

“Today we are turning the page on green hydrogen pilot projects and moving into the chapter of large-scale construction.”

In comments to ‘Euronews’, Wetselaar argued that ‘Onuba’ can help reinforce Spain’s role in Europe’s energy transition and reduce external dependence.

He explained,

We need European energy that is decarbonised and produced by us, and that is exactly what this project delivers,

Spain has abundant solar energy, very good wind power and space to build large-scale renewables

Maarten Wetselaar

Moeve’s chief executive

The company expects the facility to produce around 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen a year, avoiding some 250,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually. The hydrogen will be used to support more sustainable production of fuels for road, air and maritime transport, as well as contributing to the decarbonisation of other industries.

Sánchez hails construction of the plant

The start of construction was marked on Thursday in Palos de la Frontera at an event bringing together representatives of the Spanish government, the European Commission, the regional government of Andalusia and the town councils of Palos de la Frontera and Huelva, along with executives from the companies involved in the project.

Among those attending were the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, the president of the regional government of Andalusia, Juanma Moreno, the third deputy prime minister and minister for the Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, and the European Commission’s executive vice-president for a Clean, Fair and Competitive Transition, Teresa Ribera.

The prime minister welcomed what he described as a “huge industrial opportunity” which, in addition to creating jobs, shows that “the energy transition is already driving investment”, both public and private.

He said at the event,

For decades, Spain and Europe have depended too heavily on energy coming from elsewhere.

”We still do. Unfortunately, every international crisis reminds us of the huge price we are paying for that dependence. We cannot leave our supply at the mercy of unjustified wars, of tensions elsewhere, of the legitimate geopolitical interests of other powers that are not our own, nor, of course, keep picking up the tab for those who turn energy into just another piece in their power games.”

Spain at the heart of production

For Moeve, Spain’s conditions, and those of Andalusia in particular, offer an advantage for the development of green hydrogen. The company highlights the availability of solar and wind power, land for large renewable facilities and conditions that make it possible to produce renewable electricity at competitive cost.

Wetselaar said,

Spain has abundant solar energy, very good wind power and space to build large renewable parks,

In his view, given that renewable electricity accounts for a large share of the cost of producing green hydrogen, the availability of renewable resources could make the country one of Europe’s leading producers.

The ‘Onuba’ project is led by Moeve, which holds a 51% stake in the initiative. Hy24 and Cofides together hold 29%, while Enagás Renovable and Alter Enersun control the remaining 20%.

The project has been recognised by the European Union as a Project of Common Interest and has received €304 million in funding from the Spanish government through the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, financed by the European Union via NextGenerationEU.

title: $700/t Carbon Price Needed Before New Fuels Take Most of Shipping's Bunker Demand
description:
In the study's base case, a Tier 2 penalty of $380/tCO2e under the IMO's Net-Zero Framework, conventional fuel oil with onboard carbon capture remains the cheapest option through mid-century, and it takes a price of $700/tCO2e by 2050 before new fuels, including drop-ins, reach 61% of fleet energy consumption.
The study finds no clear cost winner between e-methanol and e-ammonia: ammonia is cheaper to produce, but crew training, exclusion zones, and specialised bunkering largely cancel that out, leaving the two near parity through 2050.
Upstream Signposts What decides between them is upstream.
The bio-methanol cost trajectory and the regulatory treatment of food-crop biofuels, which decides ethanol's competitiveness, are the other signposts it flags, noting that EU rules cover only around 20% of international shipping's energy demand.
BCG managing director and senior partner Anand Veeraraghavan said the transition is being shaped as much by policy and cost uncertainty as by technology readiness.
text:
At $380/tCO2e, methanol dual-fuel engines reach about 10% of fleet capacity but methanol supplies only about 2% of fleet energy by 2050

At $700/tCO2e, new fuels including drop-ins reach 61% of consumption

E-methanol and e-ammonia end up near cost parity once ammonia's handling costs are counted

Liquid fuels favour today's bunkering hubs; ammonia could create production-linked and import hubs

Fitting a ship with a dual-fuel engine says little about what it will burn: under the carbon penalty currently proposed at the IMO, methanol engines would be on around 10% of the world fleet's capacity by 2050 while methanol itself supplied only about 2% of the fleet's energy, according to a new study by the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) and Boston Consulting Group (BCG).

The report, Navigating the Maritime Fuel Transition, models 12 fuel pathways and six engine configurations to 2050, and its central finding is that dual-fuel engines let owners switch back to conventional fuel whenever it is cheaper, so fuel economics rather than engine choice decide what ships consume, GCMD said in an emailed announcement on Thursday.

In the study's base case, a Tier 2 penalty of $380/tCO2e under the IMO's Net-Zero Framework, conventional fuel oil with onboard carbon capture remains the cheapest option through mid-century, and it takes a price of $700/tCO2e by 2050 before new fuels, including drop-ins, reach 61% of fleet energy consumption.

The timing matters because the fleet renews at about 4% a year and more than half the ships in service in 2050 will come from orders placed before 2035, with GCMD chief executive Lynn Loo saying owners are making long-lived engine choices before the relative economics of future fuels are clear.

The study finds no clear cost winner between e-methanol and e-ammonia: ammonia is cheaper to produce, but crew training, exclusion zones, and specialised bunkering largely cancel that out, leaving the two near parity through 2050.

Upstream Signposts

What decides between them is upstream. Green hydrogen at $2/kg rather than $3/kg by 2050 lifts the combined methanol and ammonia share of fleet demand to 36% from 4%, while biogenic CO2 costing $150/t rather than $50/t cuts methanol's share to 14% from 23% and lifts ammonia's to 22% from 14%, the report finds.

The bio-methanol cost trajectory and the regulatory treatment of food-crop biofuels, which decides ethanol's competitiveness, are the other signposts it flags, noting that EU rules cover only around 20% of international shipping's energy demand.

Bunker Hubs

For the bunker industry, the report's view is that liquid fuels such as methanol and ethanol reinforce the established hubs because they are straightforward to move and deliver, while ammonia could produce two new kinds of port: production-linked hubs competing on cheap fuel, and import-aggregation hubs competing on scale by pooling maritime demand with industry and power.

BCG managing director and senior partner Anand Veeraraghavan said the transition is being shaped as much by policy and cost uncertainty as by technology readiness.

text:
The timing is significant, as the industry begins testing how ammonia can be supplied to ships in practice, the IMO is simultaneously developing the safety framework needed to support its wider use. In May, the IMO Maritime Safety Committee approved interim guidelines for ships using ammonia as fuel, alongside interim training guidelines for seafarers working aboard ammonia-fuelled vessels. That work continued on 17 September with an IMO technical seminar addressing ammonia production and supply, bunkering, onboard technologies, spill response, safety and ammonia effluents.

Against that backdrop, the world-first STS operation was completed on the same day at a quay within Japan Marine United Corporation’s Ariake Shipyard. Ammonia was transferred from the ammonia carrier Shoei Maru to an ammonia-fuelled medium gas carrier (AFMGC), scheduled for delivery in November 2026, ahead of the vessel’s sea trials using fuel ammonia.

The operation involved NYK Line, Japan Marine United Corporation, Nihon Shipyard Co., Ltd., Mitsubishi Gas Chemical Company, Inc. and Kokuka Sangyo Co., Ltd.

Testing the bunkering challenge

Ammonia is increasingly being considered as a potential marine fuel because it produces no CO₂ during combustion. That gives it a potential role in efforts to reduce emissions from international shipping. But its potential as a fuel comes with a major operational challenge.

Ammonia is toxic, making its handling and transfer considerably more demanding than conventional marine fuels. Developing reliable procedures for moving it between vessels will therefore be an important part of building the infrastructure needed to support ammonia-fuelled shipping.

As more ammonia-fuelled vessels enter service, the industry will need more than ships capable of using the fuel. It will also need a dependable supply chain, appropriate bunkering infrastructure and operating procedures that can manage the hazards associated with ammonia.

STS bunkering could form part of that future infrastructure, particularly where fuel needs to be transferred directly between vessels.

The experience gained from the operation therefore provides practical knowledge that can inform future ammonia bunkering operations as the technology moves closer to commercial deployment. The AFMGC involved in the operation is in the final stage of construction and is scheduled for delivery in November 2026.

title: Cyprus joins Mediterranean four as EU rift deepens over IMO shipping rules
description:
The report said Cyprus, Italy and Malta had also voiced reservations during European discussions, placing the four Mediterranean shipping countries increasingly on the same side of the argument.
The regulations would initially apply to ocean-going ships above 5,000 gross tonnage, which the IMO says account for more than 85 per cent of global shipping emissions.
The Greek ministry said the four countries would seek closer coordination with the aim of safeguarding the competitiveness of European shipping.
That leaves Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Malta only a matter of weeks to turn the political coordination agreed in Limassol into detailed negotiating positions.
For Cyprus in particular, the debate is no longer simply about backing an international emissions target.
text:
Cyprus has emerged as part of a four-country Mediterranean bloc pressing for changes to the proposed global shipping decarbonisation framework, as divisions between major maritime states and Brussels deepen ahead of crucial negotiations at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

The disagreement has sharpened in recent weeks, with Greece, Cyprus, Italy and Malta raising concerns over the economic consequences of the proposed rules, particularly the cost of alternative fuels, emissions pricing and the competitiveness of European shipping.

Newmoney reported on Friday, citing Euractiv, that the European Commission was pressing for a united EU position ahead of the next round of IMO negotiations, while Greece continued to resist the current approach.

The report said Cyprus, Italy and Malta had also voiced reservations during European discussions, placing the four Mediterranean shipping countries increasingly on the same side of the argument.

Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euractiv that European unity at the IMO was “imperative”, adding that the expectation was for the “European family” to be on the same page.

He did not, however, say whether the Commission could take action against Greece if Athens were again to depart from the agreed EU line.

Euractiv reported that Greece, Cyprus, Italy and Malta did not sign up to the final EU agreement reached in late August, while Greece has also been involved in discussions with the US Saudi Arabia and other countries over alternative approaches to the proposed framework.

The disagreement centres on the IMO Net-Zero Framework, which would introduce a global marine fuel standard alongside a greenhouse gas emissions pricing mechanism.

Under the current draft, ships would have to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy they use, measured across the full fuel lifecycle from production to consumption.

Ships exceeding the prescribed limits would have to compensate through surplus units or by purchasing so-called remedial units through the proposed IMO Net-Zero Fund.

For the 2028-2030 reporting period, the draft framework sets the initial price of Tier 1 remedial units at $100 per tonne of CO2 equivalent, with Tier 2 units priced at $380 per tonne. Those figures remain part of a framework that is still under negotiation and could therefore change before adoption.

The regulations would initially apply to ocean-going ships above 5,000 gross tonnage, which the IMO says account for more than 85 per cent of global shipping emissions.

For shipowners, the consequences go well beyond environmental compliance.

The eventual shape of the rules could influence which fuels ships use, the economics of LNG and other transition fuels, investment in zero and near-zero-emission technologies, fleet renewal and decisions over whether existing vessels should be upgraded or replaced.

The issue has therefore become particularly important for Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Malta, whose shipping sectors leave them heavily exposed to changes in international maritime regulation.

Only last week, the four countries formalised closer cooperation during a ministerial meeting in Limassol, where they signed a joint declaration committing themselves to closer coordination ahead of discussions at both EU and IMO level.

The September 9 meeting brought together Shipping Deputy Minister Marina Hadjimanolis, Greek Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy Minister Vassilis Kikilias and Malta’s Sustainable Mobility Minister Chris Bonett, while Italian Deputy Infrastructure and Transport Minister Edoardo Rixi took part remotely.

The four governments agreed to coordinate more closely on the competitiveness of European shipping and decarbonisation, creating a common platform ahead of the next major international negotiations.

As previously reported, Hadjimanolis stressed after the meeting that the initiative was not intended to undermine EU unity, but said some maritime issues affected major shipping states more directly than others.

She said the four countries were “ready to lead together this change”.

Italy’s ambassador to Cyprus Antonella Cavallari said at the same meeting that the four countries together represented 75 per cent of the EU fleet, arguing that this gave them considerable collective weight when maritime rules were being discussed.

Kikilias, meanwhile, linked the issue directly to the wider European economy, warning that decisions affecting shipping could ultimately feed through into energy, food and consumer prices.

His ministry said ahead of the Limassol meeting that particular attention would be paid to the IMO decarbonisation negotiations and to the forthcoming revision of the EU Emissions Trading System for shipping. The Greek ministry said the four countries would seek closer coordination with the aim of safeguarding the competitiveness of European shipping.

The four-country coordination has taken on added significance following the latest IMO negotiating round in London.

The IMO’s latest working group on greenhouse gas emissions met from September 1 to 4, with nearly 1,200 participants, but several major questions remained unresolved.

Delegates discussed proposals aimed at addressing concerns surrounding the draft amendments to Marpol Annex VI, but the group called for further consultations before the next meeting.

Rather than producing agreed text for the Marine Environment Protection Committee, the group deferred further consideration of the outstanding proposals to its next session in November, when delegates will again attempt to narrow the differences surrounding the Net-Zero Framework.

The treatment of different fuels is particularly important because LNG and other transition fuels have become one of the points of disagreement between countries involved in the talks.

The wider IMO climate strategy calls for the uptake of zero or near-zero greenhouse gas fuels, technologies and energy sources to reach at least 5 per cent, striving for 10 per cent, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030, while pursuing net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from the sector by or around 2050.

The Commission continues publicly to support that overall objective.

Following the IMO’s MEPC 84 meeting in May, the European Commission said it remained firmly behind the goal of global shipping reaching net-zero emissions by 2050 and would continue working with other parties towards an ambitious international framework.

However, Euractiv reported this week that differences remain not only between member states, but also over how far the existing framework should be altered to win wider international support.

A senior EU diplomat told the publication that negotiations could potentially slip into 2027, while Euractiv also reported differences within the Commission itself over how accommodating the EU should be towards LNG.

The publication said the Commission’s transport department, DG MOVE, was pushing for what it described as a more “realistic” agreement, while DG CLIMA maintained that LNG should not be recognised as a clean fuel.

The next negotiating window is now tightly packed.

The ISWG-GHG 23 working group will meet from November 23 to 27, followed immediately by MEPC 85 from November 30 to December 3.

The IMO’s extraordinary Marine Environment Protection Committee session, which was adjourned in October 2025 after governments failed to reach agreement on formal adoption of the framework, is scheduled to resume on December 4, subject to the outcome of MEPC 85.

That leaves Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Malta only a matter of weeks to turn the political coordination agreed in Limassol into detailed negotiating positions. For Cyprus in particular, the debate is no longer simply about backing an international emissions target.

text:
The Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization, Mr. Arsenio Dominguez, has called on Member States to refrain from actions that endanger merchant ships and put seafarers’ lives at risk.

Addressing the IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers, the Secretary-General warned of the severe impacts of geopolitical tensions on the shipping industry.

Secretary-General Dominguez said: “We are reaching a point where these conflicts are being used as a pretext to attack merchant vessels and innocent seafarers. Do not use these conflicts to attack innocent seafarers.”

Since the current conflict in the Middle East began on 28 February, IMO has verified 80 attacks on international shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in the deaths of at least 22 seafarers and injuries to many others.

In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, dozens of fatalities have reportedly resulted from attacks on international shipping in recent months, although precise numbers are difficult to verify.

Attacks in the Red Sea have also resumed, with four fatalities confirmed in the latest attack by the Houthis on a merchant vessel on 11 August.

Secretary-General Dominguez emphasized that the attacks across these conflicts are not attributable to one single actor: “In the Strait of Hormuz, it is not only one country attacking merchant vessels. In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, it is not only one country attacking merchant vessels.”

He underlined that addressing the root causes of these geopolitical conflicts is beyond IMO’s remit, but that their impact is increasingly evident across global maritime trade and shipping operations. He urged delegates to raise these impacts on international shipping with their governments and in the appropriate international fora. When shipping operations are disrupted, the consequences extend far beyond the maritime sector, affecting economies, supply chains and everyday lives.

“I call on you to share these impacts with the relevant bodies in your countries so that this can be dealt with within the United Nations, as appropriate.… It falls to you and your capitals, and relevant bodies of the United Nations, to address the root causes and find solutions,” he emphasized.

IMO Secretariat stands ready to contribute to workable solutions for the shipping industry that Member States can bring forward at the technical and operational level.

The Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers meets in London from 14 to 18 September to discuss safety issues related to the transport of dangerous goods, bulk cargoes and containers by sea.

description:

Engine Emission Test Plan becomes central A key part of the new procedure is the Engine Emission Test Plan.
This gives operators a more defined framework for demonstrating compliance without requiring testing arrangements that may be impractical for an installed engine.
For owners planning an engine modification, the NOx certification implications should be addressed early in the retrofit process, rather than once the technical work has been completed.

text:
The amendments to the NOx Technical Code 2008, adopted through IMO Resolution MEPC.398(83), entered into force internationally on 1 September 2026. The Norwegian Maritime Authority (NMA) has also incorporated the requirements into its national regulatory framework.

The change addresses the practical challenge of certifying engines that are already installed onboard and subsequently modified.

Under the new framework, the certification procedure can be applied to an Individual Engine or an Engine Group represented by a Parent Engine, but not to Engine Family certification. Where a substantial modification changes the engine’s rated power and/or rated speed, its nameplate must also be replaced accordingly.

Engine Emission Test Plan becomes central

A key part of the new procedure is the Engine Emission Test Plan.

Under MEPC.398(83), the plan must be prepared by the applicant and agreed with the Administration before the test is scheduled.

IMO has provided further guidance through MEPC.1/Circ.921, Guidance on the content of the Engine Emission test plan, which sets out the information that should be addressed in the plan. This includes details of the applicant and engine, existing and requested certification, the substantial modification involved and the arrangements for carrying out the emissions test.

The circular also requires information on whether testing will take place while the vessel is underway or in port, as well as details covering exhaust-gas measurement, engine power measurement, test-cycle load points and fuel-consumption measurement. For engines using low-flashpoint or gaseous fuels, the plan should also explain how the composition of the fuel used during testing will be determined.

IMO states that where particular arrangements require additional or alternative approaches, these should be agreed in advance with the Administration. Any later revisions to an agreed test plan should also be communicated to the Administration for consideration.

What about onboard testing?

The revised procedure is designed around the practical circumstances of testing an engine that is already installed onboard.

When setting the test-cycle load points, the point corresponding to 100% load may, subject to the agreed Engine Emission Test Plan, be set at no lower than 85% of the engine’s rated power. If that level cannot be achieved, the test must be deferred until at least that power level can be reached.

MEPC.1/Circ.921 further specifies that where maximum power during the test is not expected to reach the 90–100% maximum continuous rating range, but will remain at or above 85%, the test plan should explain why the higher range cannot be achieved, state the maximum power expected and provide justification for the declared rated power.

This gives operators a more defined framework for demonstrating compliance without requiring testing arrangements that may be impractical for an installed engine.

Why does this matter for retrofit projects?

The changes are particularly relevant as shipowners consider modifications to existing machinery as part of fleet efficiency and decarbonisation projects.

According to the NMA, engines that are, for example, converted to operate on alternative fuels or otherwise upgraded can benefit from a clearer and more practical certification pathway adapted to onboard NOx measurements. The amendments are intended to ensure that modified engines continue to comply with the applicable NOx requirements following upgrades or substantial modifications.

During Norway’s consultation, the Norwegian Coastal Shipowners Association highlighted the importance of ensuring that recertification does not become a barrier to measures involving existing tonnage, including engine upgrades, hybridisation and the transition to alternative fuels.

The NMA said the amendments should contribute to a clearer and more predictable framework for engine recertification.

However, an alternative-fuel conversion should not automatically be understood as triggering the new procedure in every case. The regulatory trigger remains whether the installed engine has undergone a substantial modification, as defined under the NOx Technical Code, or is being certified to a Tier for which it was not certified when installed.

What should shipowners consider?

For owners planning an engine modification, the NOx certification implications should be addressed early in the retrofit process, rather than once the technical work has been completed.

Operators should establish whether the proposed modification falls within the new procedure and engage with the relevant Administration or Recognised Organisation. Where section 7.2 applies, the Engine Emission Test Plan will need to be developed and agreed before the emissions test is scheduled.

Particular attention should be given to the engine’s existing certification, the intended modification, requested NOx Tier, rated power and speed, test arrangements and the ability to achieve the required load points.

The new requirements therefore provide a more defined route for modifying existing engines while demonstrating continued compliance with the applicable NOx limits under MARPOL Annex VI.

title: Shipping's Fuel Transition Hinges on a Number Nobody Has Agreed On Yet - gCaptain
description:
The study models fuel adoption out to 2050 under three regulatory scenarios, built around the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework.
Until then, shipowners are committing capital to newbuilds without knowing what carbon price they will eventually face.
Only if the penalty were to rise toward USD 700 per tonne does the economic balance tip decisively toward methanol, ammonia and ethanol.
Whichever version of the Net-Zero Framework eventually clears the IMO, the size of the carbon price looks like the single biggest lever policymakers hold.
The UK, meanwhile, extended its own emissions trading scheme to domestic shipping from 1 July 2026, adding another layer of carbon cost for operators to navigate.
text:
International shipping is being asked to decarbonize before it knows what it will burn.

By Paul Morgan (gCaptain) – Vessels capable of running on methanol, ammonia or ethanol are already entering the fleet, yet a new joint study from the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonization and Boston Consulting Group makes an uncomfortable point plain: none of these fuels is currently cheap enough to displace conventional bunkers at scale, and the regulation meant to close that gap is still being argued over.

The study models fuel adoption out to 2050 under three regulatory scenarios, built around the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework. That framework was approved in principle at MEPC 83 in April 2025, but its formal adoption was pushed back by a full year when member states failed to reach agreement at an extraordinary session that October, following vocal opposition from Washington. The vote has now been rescheduled for 4 December 2026, straight after the IMO’s MEPC 85 session. Until then, shipowners are committing capital to newbuilds without knowing what carbon price they will eventually face.

That price turns out to matter more than almost anything else in the model. Held at the level currently on the table, USD 380 per tonne of CO2 equivalent, the study finds conventional fuel oil paired with onboard carbon capture remains the cheapest compliant option through mid-century, and the fleet stays dominated by fossil fuels. Only if the penalty were to rise toward USD 700 per tonne does the economic balance tip decisively toward methanol, ammonia and ethanol. Whichever version of the Net-Zero Framework eventually clears the IMO, the size of the carbon price looks like the single biggest lever policymakers hold.

IMO Net-Zero Framework Holds Ground After Latest Round of Climate Talks

Regional rules cannot substitute for that global signal, at least not on their own. The EU’s emissions trading system and FuelEU Maritime Regulation together cover only around a fifth of international shipping’s energy use, since they apply solely to voyages touching European ports. Outside that pool, according to the modelling, the fleet simply carries on burning what is cheapest. Brussels appears to have registered as much: on 17 July 2026, the European Commission proposed a revision to its ETS that would reserve up to 110 million emissions allowances between 2028 and 2040 specifically to subsidise the extra cost of low- and zero-emission marine fuels, an implicit admission that regulatory pressure alone was not shifting the economics fast enough. The UK, meanwhile, extended its own emissions trading scheme to domestic shipping from 1 July 2026, adding another layer of carbon cost for operators to navigate.

Two fuels emerge from the analysis as the leading long-term candidates, and neither has a clear advantage over the other. E-ammonia is cheaper to produce than e-methanol, but that saving is largely eaten up by the cost of handling a toxic, refrigerated cargo: specialist storage, larger exclusion zones, additional crew training and more complex bunkering all add up. E-methanol is simpler to handle but needs a sustainable carbon source, and the price of that biogenic CO2 turns out to be the swing factor. The study finds that below roughly USD 150 per tonne of biogenic CO2, methanol tends to win out on cost; above it, ammonia does. For both fuels, though, the price of green hydrogen remains the dominant input, accounting for more than half of the total cost of fuel use out to 2050.

There is a live data point that hints at how quickly this could move. In March 2026, engine maker WinGD and renewable energy group Envision Energy published a study of ammonia bunkering economics on the China-to-Australia route, using a real bunker price of USD 710 per tonne sourced from Envision’s Jinzhou production facility. At that price, the two companies calculated that ammonia-fuelled bulk carriers and container ships could already undercut equivalent VLSFO-powered vessels on operating cost over the first compliance period of the IMO framework. It is one route, one supplier and one moment in a volatile market, but it suggests the cost curve the GCMD-BCG model anticipates for the 2030s may already be visible at the margins today.

IMO Urged to Give Shipping Clear Investment Signal on Net Zero Pathway

Ethanol’s prospects, by contrast, look almost entirely dependent on a single regulatory decision. First-generation, food-crop-based ethanol is currently cost-competitive and available at scale, and the study credits it with supplying close to a tenth of the fleet’s energy needs by 2050 under neutral treatment. But the EU’s FuelEU Maritime Regulation already excludes food-crop biofuels from favourable treatment, assigning them the emissions factor of the dirtiest available fossil pathway instead. If that stance were applied globally, the study finds ethanol’s contribution would collapse to near zero, with the lost volume absorbed almost entirely by conventional fuel oil rather than by other alternatives. The fuel’s future, in other words, rests less on its chemistry than on how regulators choose to classify its feedstock.

On the technical side, there is encouraging evidence that engine flexibility is real rather than theoretical. Maersk’s methanol-fuelled Laura Maersk completed a full trial on 100 per cent ethanol earlier this year, building on earlier blend tests, and confirmed the fuel could be burned without compromising engine performance. That matters for the study’s central argument about optionality: dual-fuel engines let owners hedge against an uncertain fuel market, switching between compatible new fuels and conventional bunkers as prices move. But the same flexibility cuts both ways. The study shows a persistent gap between engine capacity and actual fuel consumption, with methanol dual-fuel engines making up a tenth of the projected 2050 fleet while methanol itself supplies barely two per cent of energy consumed, because owners keep the option to burn cheaper conventional fuel instead.

That gap is arguably the report’s most important finding for anyone chartering, building or financing ships today. Ordering a dual-fuel vessel does not guarantee the new fuel gets burned. Vessels last 25 to 30 years and only around 4 per cent of the global fleet turns over annually, so the engines ordered in the next few years will still be sailing in 2050 regardless of how the regulatory picture eventually settles. The study’s advice—that fleet strategy should be built around optionality rather than commitment to a single fuel—reads less like a bet on any particular winner and more like an acknowledgment that nobody, including the modellers, yet knows which fuel that will be.

The bunkering map is expected to shift unevenly as a result. Liquid fuels such as methanol and ethanol travel relatively easily, so existing hubs like Singapore and the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp region are likely to extend their dominance simply by importing whichever new fuel their customers need. Ammonia is a different proposition. Its toxicity and low boiling point make long-distance transport expensive, which the study argues will split future ammonia bunkering into two distinct types of port: those sitting next to cheap domestic production, and those with enough existing vessel traffic to aggregate demand and justify import infrastructure through scale alone. Which type wins in any given region will depend on decisions being taken now about where hydrogen and ammonia plants get built and which ports choose to commit to the infrastructure first.

For an industry that prizes long asset lives and long-term charters, the honest conclusion is that 2050’s fuel mix is still being decided, not by any single technology breakthrough, but by a carbon price that has yet to be agreed, a biogenic CO2 market that barely exists yet, and a series of regulatory classifications still working their way through Brussels and London. The vessels ordered over the next few years will have to live with whatever answer eventually emerges.

text:
The World Shipping Council (WSC) has called on governments to close a gap in international dangerous goods regulations that allows containers carrying thousands of lithium batteries to be transported without informing carriers about the hazard.

The organisation has raised the matter amid increasing global battery transport and persistent cargo fire risk at sea.

International Energy Agency data shows that global lithium-ion battery deployment in 2025 was six times higher than in 2020 and battery demand is expected to double by 2030. Insurer Allianz has estimated that a fire occurs aboard a container ship approximately every 17 days.

At the centre of the concern is Special Provision 188 of the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) Code.

The provision exempts small lithium batteries from certain dangerous-goods requirements when they meet specified testing, packaging and capacity criteria. However, it does not limit the number of exempt batteries that may be consolidated in a single container.

According to the WSC, a container carrying around 4 200 laptops could contain approximately 416 kilowatt-hours of stored energy – equivalent to the battery capacity of three or four electric vehicles – without requiring dangerous goods documentation or container placarding.

“A container can be packed with thousands of lithium batteries and still travel without a dangerous goods declaration,” said WSC President and CEO Joe Kramek.

“The SP188 exemption intends to simplify the transport of individual devices with small batteries, not to make entire container loads invisible.”

The WSC said lithium batteries are transported safely every day when they are properly declared and the associated risks are managed.

However, when carriers are not informed of the cargo, they cannot properly assess the risk, select an appropriate stowage position, separate the container from other cargo or prepare an informed emergency response.

“We know what can happen when hazards are invisible,” Kramek said.

“Batteries shipped under the exemption have caused serious container fires, putting people, ports, ships and the marine environment at risk.”

The WSC, supported by five governments and a coalition of industry organisations, has submitted a paper to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) outlining a potential container-level threshold.

Battery shipments exceeding the threshold will have to be declared and could also be subject to placarding requirements.

“The current rules are not working as intended,” Kramek said.

“As battery shipments continue to grow, we need a better solution that makes these cargoes visible and allows the risks to be properly managed.”

The IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers is considering the issue at a meeting in London.

The WSC has urged the sub-committee to address the matter as a priority so that improved regulations can be incorporated into Amendment 44-28 of the IMDG Code scheduled to become mandatory on January 1, 2030.

title: Are UK and Cyprus Ministers in synch over decarbonisation? - Seatrade Maritime News
description:
Speaking at Tuesday’s Capital Link Conference both Ministers agreed that providing the right regulatory framework for industry to innovate is the process by which maritime decarbonisation can be delivered.
The discussion offered a fleeting look at the strings being pulled to guide governments in their decarbonisation discussions.
Britain’s junior minister focused on autonomy and nuclear power, going as far as name checking a company, Ocean Infinity and a technology, maritime nuclear power.
“The UK is clear that in order to decarbonise, we need to be exploring a range of decarbonisation measures in shipping, especially in regards to future fuels.
The discussion at Capital Link offers a brief glimpse to the complexity that liberal democracies bring to decarbonisation negotiations.
text:
Cypriot Deputy Shipping Minister, Marina Hadjimanolis, and Keir Mather, the UK’s Transport Minister agreed on stage in London, must work with the maritime industry to deliver a workable and pragmatic decarbonisation of a hard to abate sector.

Speaking at Tuesday’s Capital Link Conference both Ministers agreed that providing the right regulatory framework for industry to innovate is the process by which maritime decarbonisation can be delivered.

But there was a tension amongst the on-stage camaraderie. Though If your ears could blink, you’d miss the distinction.

The discussion offered a fleeting look at the strings being pulled to guide governments in their decarbonisation discussions.

Britain’s junior minister focused on autonomy and nuclear power, going as far as name checking a company, Ocean Infinity and a technology, maritime nuclear power.

Conversely Hadjimanolis talked about the key role of seafarers and the “pragmatic” measures needed for “a realistic [IMO Net Zero Framework] measure, we want a measure that will give stability to the shipowners.”

Hadjimanolis’ language is reminiscent of the Greek shipowners’ who argue that the pragmatic path to decarbonisation is to use the fuel that is readily available until a workable and affordable alternative is found.

For Greek shipowners that pragmatic fuel is LNG, a fossil fuel.

It so happens that Cyprus has relatively recently discovered large reserves of the gas off its southern coast. A fact that Hadjimanolis alluded to when discussing the country’s stance ahead of the Extraordinary Session of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) last year.

Unlike Cyprus, the UK’s gas reserves are largely spent, but its nuclear expertise is an industry that can offer emission free, clean, shipping at the point of use.

Asked about the lifecycle emissions and costs of uranium as a nuclear fuel the Minister told Seatrade Maritime News in a conversation: “Obviously, nuclear in shipping is an emerging technology, the UK has got a really robust rules-based system for a lot of the issues concerned with nuclear power, whether that be waste disposal, but we need to adapt and create new regulations to ensure that nuclear shipping can be something that the UK has a share of in the future.”

All concerns said Mather around nuclear as a maritime fuel need to be “robustly worked through” in discussions at the IMO and that any regulation of maritime nuclear power must be global and agreed at the UN body.

“The UK is clear that in order to decarbonise, we need to be exploring a range of decarbonisation measures in shipping, especially in regards to future fuels. We want to be part of that work, to realise the enormous opportunity that's there,” added Mather.

What is clear, and unites the two ministers, is that their comments on emissions control and clean fuels are secondary to requirement of boosting national income.

Cyprus officials argued last year that it was likely that Cyprus would vote against the NZF, in defiance of a pan-EU agreement, while in the UK the Labour government could still tarnish its green credentials by approving new drilling in the North Sea for oil and gas.

Meanwhile, Mather’s mention of Ocean Infinity was no slip of the tongue. The company is a technology company that specialises amongst other things in seabed mapping and autonomous vessels, such as the Kuwaiti Coast Guard’s Needlefish uncrewed surface vessel (USV).

“The UK also needs to not be shy and to be unashamedly competitive,” said Mather, “In terms of capturing market shares in what is definitely going to define the future of maritime innovation in decades to come, and I see that particularly being in autonomous shipping.”

Hadjimanolis, however, stressed the importance of Cyprus’ history in shipping forming part of the country’s valued identity, which can be found in its people.

Shipping as an entity is its people stressed Hadjimanolis, contradicting Mather’s pitch for uncrewed vessel developments.

Moderator Dora Mace-Kokota, a partner at Stephenson Harwood, noted Hadjimanolis’ comments, adding that a maritime nation is about its people: “It's also a nation that remembers and knows how to regulate and then how to act as a maritime nation,” she added, turning to Mather to ask if he had any more specific thoughts in terms of initiatives.

Mather, however, ignored the discussion on the workforce: “The first thing is that the government needs to show that we're putting our money where our mouth is in terms of the sort of direction that we want to encourage private sector companies to work with us to make those big bets about where the future of shipping and maritime is moving.”

UK government maritime proposals are about technological fixes, because London is focused on growth and developing industry is key to growth.

In Cyprus with its major shipping related companies being ship management, the largest ship management cluster in Europe according to the minister, the focus is more on crew and staffing levels.

The discussion at Capital Link offers a brief glimpse to the complexity that liberal democracies bring to decarbonisation negotiations.

It is not that Ministers are being dishonest, it is that they are viewing the challenges from their own side of the black hole, and from that unique viewpoint they are focusing on jobs and wealth.

From a climate scientists’ point of view the focus is emissions reduction and the most efficient means to achieve that, while industry is there to make money and those views of the abyss offer their own challenges.

To avoid the inevitable crash through the event horizon, with humanity disappearing, industry, government and scientists must find a system of growth that brings these competing views into a genuinely green solution for our climate.

title: Rødne Takes Delivery of New All-Electric Catamaran From Oma
description:
The vessel is 46 meters long, 11 meters wide and has a service speed of 19 knots.
"We are very satisfied with the cooperation with Oma and the delivery of the new boat.
Choosing a local Norwegian shipyard with Norwegian subcontractors gives us the security and predictability we depend on," says Lars Rødne, CEO of Rødne.
"This is our first delivery to Rødne, and we greatly appreciate the trust they have shown us.
The project is a good example of value creation that occurs when Norwegian shipping companies choose Norwegian shipyards and Norwegian suppliers," says Gunnar Jan Oma, CEO of Oma.
text:
The new combi-catamaran combines high efficiency, flexibility and sustainability. The vessel is 46 meters long, 11 meters wide and has a service speed of 19 knots. It has the capacity to transport both trucks, passenger cars and up to 97 passengers, while also being adapted for cargo handling.

M/S Rygerlys is designed to offer high comfort, and is equipped with a modern, all-electric propulsion system that enables emission-free operation on the entire route. The delivery is an important contribution to the development of more sustainable maritime transport and underlines the maritime industry's role in the green transition.

"We are very satisfied with the cooperation with Oma and the delivery of the new boat. Choosing a local Norwegian shipyard with Norwegian subcontractors gives us the security and predictability we depend on," says Lars Rødne, CEO of Rødne. "This is also of great importance after the takeover. Proximity to the shipyard, short distances and good accessibility give us security for safe operation and high regularity. This benefits both the company and the travelers ."

A Norwegian collaborative project

The vessel, made of recyclable and seawater-resistant aluminum, was built entirely at Oma Baatbyggeri in Stord in close collaboration with around 20 Norwegian subcontractors. Several local companies played a role in the construction process.

Teca AS in Stord was responsible for the installation of the electrical system, as well as the radio and navigation equipment. Servogear from Bømlo supplied the vessel's gear and propeller system, while Fjellstrand in Hardanger contributed to the construction of hull sections. Brunvoll from Tokke in Telemark has been responsible for the integration of the electric hybrid propulsion system and the vessel's monitoring system. In addition, a number of other, mainly Norwegian suppliers have been involved.

"This is our first delivery to Rødne, and we greatly appreciate the trust they have shown us. The project is a good example of value creation that occurs when Norwegian shipping companies choose Norwegian shipyards and Norwegian suppliers," says Gunnar Jan Oma, CEO of Oma.

Rygerlys has now arrived in Forsand. Here, a period of running-in and testing of the charging infrastructure and quays inland in the Lysefjord awaits, to ensure that the vessel meets all requirements for safety, quality and regularity before it is put into service.

title: Does the EU's Emissions Trading System 〈ETS〉 match reality?
description:

text:
Freight intelligence platform VesselBot’s recent Decoding Maritime Emissions Q2 2026 report revealed that higher levels of vessel utilization aboard containerships are among the most important factors in reducing shipping emissions.

The company followed this by publishing a new case study, EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Surcharges vs. Actual Voyage Exposure: What Shipment Execution Data Reveals.

The study applied the same voyage-level dataset used in the earlier report to a new question: whether carrier EU ETS surcharges match the actual regulatory exposure of the voyages generating them.

One of the main takeaways was that only shipment-execution data allows accurate benchmarking of ETS exposure. The study found that, for the same carrier, origin and EU destination, the actual regulatory cost can swing by an order of magnitude depending on port sequence, not distance.

On one route, a single UK port call before entering the EU—the UK is no longer a member of the 27-member bloc—cut the voyage’s actual ETS exposure to less than 1% of total emissions, while the published surcharge on that route stayed fixed.

More Than 20,000 Containership Voyages in Q2

But first, a reminder that the EU ETS is a carbon-pricing mechanism that requires shipping companies to purchase and surrender allowances for their greenhouse gas emissions.

Maritime transport has been included in the system since January 2024. For containerships, the EU ETS covers 100% of emissions from voyages between EU/EEA (European Economic Area) ports and 50% of emissions from voyages between EU/EEA and non-EU/EEA ports.

During the second quarter of 2026, more than 20,000 containership voyages fell within the scope of the EU ETS, either departing from or arriving at an EU/EEA port. Together, these voyages generated more than 11.8 million tonnes of CO₂e, of which 7.15 million tonnes, or 60%, were subject to allowance surrender.

With EU Allowances trading at around €80 per tonne at the end of the quarter, the allowances required to cover these emissions represented an estimated €572.4 million in carbon costs for Q2 alone.

Exposure on a Per-TEU Basis

For shippers, this means millions of euros in carbon costs may be incorporated into freight rates through EU ETS surcharges. It raises the question of how carriers are passing on these costs and whether the surcharges being charged actually reflect their underlying EU ETS exposure, VesselBot noted.

With the overall exposure in Q2 2026 exceeding €572 million, VesselBot asked what this translated to on a per-TEU basis.

Using a digital-twin model, it estimated that during the Q2 containership voyages within the scope of its analysis, 42.8 million TEUs were collectively carried, putting the estimated EU ETS exposure at approximately €13.40 per TEU.

“This figure should be treated as a directional benchmark rather than a shipment-level truth. Voyage-level TEU volumes do not represent unique containers: the same container can be counted on multiple legs as it moves through a carrier’s network, for example, Shanghai to Singapore, Singapore to Rotterdam, and Rotterdam to Hamburg,” VesselBot explained.

A single container therefore appears several times in the fleetwide transport-work calculation, while the shipper ultimately faces one surcharge tied to one specific origin and destination.

Isolating Voyages

Translating fleetwide exposure into a shipper-relevant benchmark therefore requires shipment-level execution data, and VesselBot got closer to this by isolating voyages whose origin-destination pairs do not overlap with one another.

For example, CMA CGM’s direct Singapore–Rotterdam, Singapore–Valencia and Singapore–Piraeus voyages provided a more accurate benchmark: an actual ETS cost of roughly €26–€31 per TEU, well below the carrier’s published surcharge of €56–€70 per TEU.

This did not mean that the difference between estimated ETS exposure and a carrier’s published surcharge represented an overcharge, VesselBot was swift to point out.

Energy-transition surcharges may also incorporate FuelEU Maritime costs and other carrier-specific commercial assumptions. It does mean, however, that the published surcharge alone cannot tell procurement teams whether its ETS component is proportionate to the regulatory exposure generated by a specific shipment.

“Instead, the comparison demonstrates the value of a route-specific ETS benchmark. It gives procurement teams a way to quantify how much of the published surcharge can be explained by the estimated EU ETS exposure generated by the underlying voyage, and to distinguish that regulatory cost from the other components bundled into the surcharge. With this benchmark, the question shifts from simply accepting the published surcharge to evaluating whether its ETS component is proportionate to how the shipment was actually executed.”

UK Port Call Changes Regulatory Treatment

Routing through a non-EU/EEA port before entering the EU changes the equation sharply. On seven observed Singapore–Felixstowe, UK–Zeebrugge voyages, VesselBot found that only 0.5% of total voyage emissions fell within the scope of the EU ETS, producing an exposure of about €5,150 per voyage—less than the surcharge collected from a single 100-TEU shipment on that route.

The pattern shows why a blanket per-TEU surcharge is a blunt instrument: The carbon cost of moving a container between two points can vary by an order of magnitude depending on routing, yet the surcharge charged to the shipper does not currently vary with it.

The question is therefore no longer simply what ETS surcharge a carrier publishes, but whether that surcharge can be benchmarked against the regulatory exposure generated by the shipment as it was actually executed.

“Answering that question requires shipment execution data that captures the vessel, routing, port sequence, emissions, utilization, and applicable ETS coverage behind each move. As carbon costs become a larger component of freight spend, this level of benchmarking will become increasingly important for organizations seeking greater control, transparency, and governance over transportation costs.”

‘Making Intelligence Operational’

Constantine Komodromos, CEO and co-founder of Greece-based VesselBot, said that more accurate emissions measurement was only the beginning.

“The real opportunity is to make that intelligence operational. Transportation is shaped by thousands of operational decisions, and the data behind those decisions has value far beyond reporting.

“Our focus is on helping organizations understand what is actually happening across their freight operations and use that understanding at both a strategic and tactical level to achieve reductions in costs and emissions.”
